What to put on a woodworking cut list

Use one row for each distinct finished part. Record its name, width, length, thickness, quantity and whether its visible grain direction must be preserved. Keep plywood, MDF, melamine and other materials on separate sheets when they cannot substitute for one another.

The table describes finished parts. Blade kerf belongs between parts in the layout, while damaged-edge or squaring allowances belong at the edge of the stock. Keeping those values separate prevents the same allowance from being counted twice.

When to move from the printable to a cut list optimizer

The blank grid is useful for a manual sketch and for checking whether the project has an obvious arrangement. It is not an exact-scale cutting diagram and does not calculate kerf, grain constraints, yield or cut order.

For a dimensioned layout, enter the same parts in the free cut list optimizer (cut list optimiser in UK spelling). For more than ten parts, multiple stock groups or grain-direction locks, Boardcut for iPhone keeps the planning workflow together.

Move the paper cut list into Boardcut

Each column on the printable maps to an input in Boardcut for iPhone, so the sheet can be the first draft of a dimensioned layout. Part name, width, length and quantity go in through a fraction keypad made for inches, with decimal-inch and millimeter modes if the plan uses them. Material and thickness decide which stock a part belongs to; Boardcut starts from standard presets such as a 4×8 plywood sheet or lets you enter the actual size of the panel you have.

The grain column becomes a per-part grain lock, and the diagram draws grain arrows so the orientation is visible before cutting. Blade kerf is drawn at its real width on every cut, with edge trim and a minimum offcut size set separately from the finished part dimensions, which matches the rule above about keeping those allowances out of the parts table.

The result is an optimized cutting diagram with a numbered cut list of every rip and crosscut linked to the drawing, plus waste, yield, sheet count, cut count and material cost. Planning is free with no piece limit and works offline. Pro adds vector PDF plans, CSV export of parts and placements, and saving usable offcuts as stock for the next project.

How to use this sheet

  1. Print one page per sheet of plywood or panel material you plan to cut.
  2. List every part you need from this sheet in the table: name, width, length, thickness, and quantity.
  3. Mark grain direction Yes or No — whether you need grain to run parallel to the long dimension of the part.
  4. Use the blank 4×8 grid below the table to sketch a rough layout: draw rectangles to represent each part and check whether the arrangement leaves avoidable gaps.
  5. Transfer the layout to the actual sheet with a pencil and straightedge before cutting.

Woodworking cut list template FAQ

Is this woodworking cut list template free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print without signup or email.

Can I use the cut list for plywood, MDF and melamine?

Yes. Record the material and thickness for each part, and plan each non-interchangeable stock type separately. Enter the actual sheet dimensions rather than assuming every product has the same usable size.

Is the 4×8 grid drawn to exact scale?

No. It is a proportional planning grid for a nominal 4×8 sheet. Write the actual stock dimensions on the page and use a dimensioned cutting diagram before cutting.

Should cut list dimensions include saw kerf?

No. Record finished part dimensions in the table and apply the measured blade kerf between parts in the layout. Keep edge-trim allowances with the stock dimensions.

Can Boardcut turn this parts list into a cutting diagram?

Yes. Boardcut for iPhone turns part and stock dimensions into a cutting diagram with kerf, grain direction, sheet count, yield and ordered cut steps. Planning is free with no piece limit; export and saved-offcut features are in Pro.
